name: Lycopene
summary: Lycopene is the red pigment that gives tomatoes, watermelon, pink grapefruit and guava their colour. It is a carotenoid, related to beta-carotene, but the body does not turn it into vitamin A. Plants make it; people get it from food.
commonUses: May work as an "internal sunscreen" that makes skin less likely to burn in the sun.
May protect the DNA in skin cells from sun damage.
May keep skin tone even and clear.
roles: Lycopene is stored in fat tissue and in organs such as the skin, adrenal glands and prostate.
Cooked and processed tomato products hold more absorbable lycopene than raw tomato, because heat and oil help release it.

foodSources.note: Processing and oil make lycopene easier to absorb.

reference.noUpperLimit: No tolerable upper intake level has been set for lycopene. EFSA's acceptable daily intake (0.5 mg per kg of body weight a day) is a safety figure for use as a food colour, not a limit for supplements. EFSA's 2026 report notes that the EU novel-food list allows up to 15 mg a day in food supplements.

cautions: Eating or taking a lot of lycopene over weeks can turn the skin orange-yellow (lycopenaemia, a harmless carotenoid skin discolouration reported in case reports), which fades after stopping; it is not jaundice, but yellow skin or eyes should still be checked by a doctor.
Lycopene does not replace sunscreen, shade or skin checks. A new or changing mole or skin spot should be looked at by a doctor, not treated with a supplement.

Supplements may come from tomato extract, a fungus fermentation or chemical synthesis, and strengths differ; EFSA has flagged that total lycopene intake from food, colours and novel foods may exceed its ADI in some groups, especially children, so keep children out of adult supplements.

People with prostate conditions, on blood-thinning or other regular medicines, or who are pregnant should check with a pharmacist or doctor before taking a supplement; no specific interaction was verified here.

origin: Lycopene is the red pigment that gives tomatoes, watermelon, pink grapefruit and guava their colour. It is a carotenoid, a fat-soluble plant pigment related to beta-carotene, but unlike beta-carotene the body does not turn it into vitamin A. Plants make it; humans cannot, so it comes from food. In the body it is stored in fat tissue and in organs such as the skin, adrenal glands and prostate.

Supplements are made from tomato extracts (oleoresin), by growing the fungus Blakeslea trispora, or by chemical synthesis. In the EU, lycopene from these sources is allowed as a food colour (E 160d) and as a novel food ingredient. Cooked and processed tomato products such as paste and sauce contain more absorbable lycopene than raw tomato, because heat and oil help release it.
dosage: There is no reference intake for lycopene. EFSA set an acceptable daily intake of 0.5 mg per kg of body weight a day for lycopene from all sources; that is a safety figure for additive use, not a target. EFSA's 2026 report notes that the EU novel-food list allows up to 15 mg of lycopene a day in food supplements, so check which source and legal basis a product uses.
An amount commonly used in studies and supplements is about 15 to 30 mg a day. This is not a reference intake or a personal recommendation.

Check the source on the label (tomato extract, a fungus called Blakeslea trispora, or synthetic) and whether the number is pure lycopene or extract weight. Lycopene dissolves in fat, so it is usually taken with a meal that contains some oil.

foodAmounts.verdict: Partly. Processed tomato products are the practical route: about 250 g of tomato sauce or 110 to 150 g of ketchup gives 15 mg, and double that gives 30 mg. Fresh tomato needs several hundred grams to over a kilogram for 15 mg. Amounts vary a lot with variety and processing, and the studies behind the supplement amounts used extracts as well as tomato products.
foodAmounts.notChecked: Lycopene is not measured in the UK food table used by this app. Values are mg per 100 g from a published review, as ranges across the studies it lists. These are amounts eaten, not absorbed; cooking with oil makes lycopene easier to absorb.
